item.title: We the People: Representation and Ratification, 1787–1791
item.snippet: 1790 population, free and enslaved; House and Senate seats in 1793; and each state's ratifying convention vote.
item.description:
Question: How did the Constitution balance large and small states, and how close was ratification?

Ideas for one lesson in MapMaker (choose any):

  • Compare free and enslaved populations in 1790 (pie charts), then switch on House seats in 1793. Every state had two senators; House seats followed population counted under the three-fifths clause. Each state's pop-up also shows its seats if enslaved people had been counted in full or not at all.
  • Switch on Ratifying the Constitution: each pie shows a convention's vote. Look for the closest votes, and for North Carolina's two conventions.
  • Sketch pins for James Madison, Alexander Hamilton, Patrick Henry and George Mason, each with a quote and the principle it argues about.
  • Download an image or export a PDF of the map to keep the work.

Notes: Today's state outlines (Natural Earth, public domain), with Maine shown as part of Massachusetts and West Virginia as part of Virginia. The 1790 census figures reproduce every state's House seats under the act of 14 April 1792, which checks them.

Sources: National Archives (seats); U.S. Census Bureau (one seat for every 33,000 people); 1790 census figures as tabulated in Wikipedia; Center for the Study of the American Constitution (votes and meeting places).

Version 1.2 (14 October 2026).

item.title: Population and House seats, 1790 to 1793
item.snippet: Each state's 1790 population, free and enslaved, and its House seats under the act of 14 April 1792.
item.description:
House seats under the apportionment act of 14 April 1792 (105 seats, one for every 33,000 people counted under the three-fifths clause), with the seats each state would have had if enslaved people had been counted in full (SeatsIfAll) or not at all (SeatsIfNone).

The 1790 census figures are as tabulated in Wikipedia's article on the 1790 census, from the Census Bureau's Heads of Families volumes. Under the act's rule they reproduce every state's seats, which checks them.

Today's state outlines (Natural Earth, public domain), with Maine shown as part of Massachusetts and West Virginia as part of Virginia.

item.title: United States Apportionment 2020
item.snippet: The process to determine how many representatives each state receives in the House of Representatives is called apportionment.
item.description:
When the founders of the United States established the government, they wanted to ensure power was separated and that there was a system of checks and balances. Therefore, the U.S. has three branches of government: the executive branch (to carry out laws), the judicial branch (to examine laws), and the legislative branch (to create the laws). 


The executive branch is led by the president, who is elected by U.S. citizens 18 years and older every four years. The president nominates justices to the Supreme Court to fill vacancies when a justice steps down or dies. The Supreme Court has had nine justices since 1869. The president also nominates court of appeals judges and district court judges. All nominated judges are confirmed by the United States Senate, as stated in the Constitution of the United States. The president and members of Congress, or the legislative branch, both serve limited terms. Congress is composed of two parts: the Senate and the House of Representatives. The Senate is composed of 100 senators, two from each of the 50 states. U.S. territories and the District of Columbia are not represented in the Senate, as they are not considered states. Each senator serves a term of six years. The House of Representatives has 435 members determined by the population of each state. Territories are not represented in the House, but the District of Columbia has an at-large representative who may not vote on issues being considered. These members each serve a term of two years.


The process to determine how many representatives each state receives is called apportionment. Every 10 years, since 1790, the United States conducts a census to tally the total number of residents (citizens, noncitizens, deployed members of the U.S. Armed Forces, and federal civilian employees stationed abroad) in each state and gather information about them and the nation’s economy. The U.S. Constitution establishes that each state must have at least one representative. The remaining 385 seats are then divided based on the method of equal proportions, which was adopted by Congress in 1941. Title 13 of the U.S. Code requires the apportionment calculation must be completed and delivered to the president within nine months of the completion of the census.


This map layer was created with data from the United States Census Bureau 2020 census. The map shows which states have gained or lost representatives since the last apportionment completed in 2010. 


Did the state you live in have a change in the number of people representing you in the House of Representatives? Do you know who your representative is?

item.title: Ratifying the Constitution, 1787 to 1791
item.snippet: Where each state's ratifying convention met, when it voted and how close the vote was.
item.description:
One point per ratifying convention at the town where it met, with the vote, the date and the building. North Carolina's first convention (Hillsborough, 1788), which voted against ratifying, has its own point.

Version 1.0 (14 October 2026).
